options: Business entities — the things, like products, dates, or customers
Events, like sales or sign-ins
Only numeric measure columns
Report layouts
questions.explain: Dimension tables describe things — products, people, places, dates — with a unique key plus descriptive columns for filtering and grouping.

options: Observations or events, like sales orders or stock movements, along with dimension keys and measures
Only text descriptions of products
A list of report filters
Copies of every dimension table's columns
questions.explain: Fact tables contain dimension key columns plus numeric measure columns, and they typically grow much larger than dimension tables over time.

questions.q: What does it mean for data to be normalized?
options: Each piece of information is stored once, referenced by a key, instead of repeated on every row
All columns are converted to numbers
Every table has exactly the same number of columns
Data is sorted alphabetically
questions.explain: Normalized data stores details like product category once in a dimension table, referenced by key — rather than repeating them on every fact row.

questions.q: What does a fact table's granularity describe?
options: The level of detail one row represents
How many dimension tables exist in the model
The total number of rows in the table
Whether the table uses Import or DirectQuery
questions.explain: Granularity is determined by the values in the dimension key columns — for example, whether each row is one sale, or a monthly total per product.

questions.q: Which pattern usually describes a raw exported CSV or Excel report?
options: Denormalized — descriptive columns like category and color repeated on every row
Already split into clean fact and dimension tables
A single dimension table with no fact table
A model with too many relationships
questions.explain: Exports are almost always one wide, denormalized table — splitting it into normalized fact and dimension tables is exactly the kind of work Power Query is for.
